title: In 2020-2025 south-east Australian stream drainage returned to its pre-1997 rate but the runoff deficit at equal rain did not shrink; a linear rain model hid it in wet years (112 gauges)
abstract: Question: after 1997, south-east Australian (SE-AU) runoff fell below its 1951-1996 rain relation, and streams drained faster at equal flow. Is faster drainage the mechanism, and did the deficit end when drainage recovered? The years 2020-2025 (wet 2020-2022, dry 2023-2025) are out of sample for all CAMELS-AUS models. Approach: 112 CAMELS-AUS v2.03 catchments (57 Victoria, 39 NSW+ACT, 16 Queensland control) with BoM daily flow 1950-2025 and SILO rain. Annual relation Q = a + bP + cP(t-1), linear (planned primary) and with a P^2 term (planned sensitivity), fitted on 1951-1996; runoff departure D (% of mean flow); loss-form index f (0 = parallel shift); recession drainage index R; four continuations fitted with data to 2019 and scored in 2020-2025; 2x2-degree cell bootstrap; plan written before any post-2021 value. Results: before 1997, the linear relation under-predicted the 5 wettest years by 27% of mean flow (95% CI 18 to 38; NSW 43%); the convex relation had no clear bias (-2%), so we prefer it (post hoc). Drainage recovered completely: R +0.23 (+0.15 to +0.31) in 2010-2019, -0.00 (-0.08 to +0.10) in 2020-2025, and near zero in the dry 2023-2025. The deficit did not shrink: SE-AU D -10.9% in 2010-2019 and -13.5% (-25.6 to -4.3) in 2020-2025; Victoria -11.3% and -10.7% (-20.0 to -4.8); wet 2020-2022 -16.5%. With the linear model NSW looked recovered in 2020-2022 (+0.4%), but the convex model gave -21.8% (CI -40 to +13). Continuing the 1997-2019 mm offset beat a return to the old relation (RMSE 4.6% of mean flow lower, 2.4 to 8.1); the refitted low post-1997 rain slope was worst in wet years. f fell from 0.25 (1997-2019) to 0.13 (2020-2025), the value of the 1959-1971 and 1983-1995 lows, but was near 0 in wet and 0.27 in dry years. In Victoria, catchments whose drainage recovered more regained more runoff (Spearman -0.65; -0.71 with rain change removed), but a drainage-independent drift of -10 points cancelled this in the mean. Conclusion: the drainage change is not what keeps SE-AU runoff low; the deficit persisted after drainage recovered. Limitations: preference for the convex model is post hoc; six out-of-sample years; wide NSW intervals; SILO rain only after 2019; rain-only annual model.

display.caption: Annual means over catchments (dots) and 3-year means (lines), 1951-2025, for Victoria, NSW+ACT and the Queensland control. Top: runoff departure from the convex 1951-1996 rain relation. Middle: drainage index R (+ = faster recession at equal flow and month). Bottom: rain anomaly. After 2020 R returns to zero, but the south-east departure stays low.

Left: before 1997, observed minus predicted runoff in each catchment's 5 wettest years when the 1957-1996 fit leaves them out; the linear relation under-predicts by 17-45% of mean flow, the convex relation does not. Right: departures in 2010-2019, 2020-2022 and 2023-2025 with both references; the NSW wet-year 'recovery' appears only with the linear reference.

Per catchment, change of drainage index R against change of runoff departure (convex) from 2010-2019 to 2020-2025. In Victoria, more drainage recovery went with more runoff recovery (Spearman -0.65), but the mean departure did not change. NSW shows no relation.

citations.reason: We use its drainage index code and test its proposal of one storage-drainage process: drainage returned by 2020-2025 but the runoff deficit did not.
We adapt its BoM download code; with another method and NSW added we also find that the Victorian deficit persisted to 2025.
Its loss of rain sensitivity is smaller with a convex reference, and the low post-1997 rain slope did not continue out of sample.
With a convex reference, the Victorian post-1997 loss form is not clearly different from the 1959-1971 low, and the 2020-2025 form equals the earlier lows.
It found that the lost share of flow grew in wet years after 1997; in the wet 2020-2022 years the deficit was a near-constant mm offset, and a linear reference inflates wet-year residuals.
It found weaker evidence for a rain-slope change; our convex reference also reduces the slope-loss estimate.
It found the rain-slope loss less certain; we add a curvature reason and an out-of-sample test.
